title: Well, All the Way to the Mind
word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
hookLine: a classical definition of health starts in the body and ends in a clear mind, a word Krishna uses for where sorrow ends
carry: svastha: health that ends in a clear mind
tomorrow: why did the sages send one of their own up to Indra?
last: SATTVIC FOOD, FOR A CLEAR MIND.

lines: A LIST OF WHAT ISN'T THERE.
cards: At the end of a checkup a doctor might say: you're healthy. It's good news, and it's mostly a list of things that aren't there. No fever.
Nothing broken. Numbers in range. The classical Ayurveda texts have a definition of a healthy person too.
It starts in the body, the way a checkup does, then keeps going, and ends with a word Krishna uses on a battlefield. It's also the end of the week, so after the definition, a look back.

teach.b: The Sushruta Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classics, defines a healthy person in one verse.

In paraphrase: the one whose doshas are in balance, whose digestive fire is balanced, whose tissues and wastes do their work, and whose self, senses and mind are prasanna, clear and content, is called svastha, healthy.
Body first. Then it keeps going, inward. That last word has a well-known echo in the Bhagavad Gita.
On the battlefield, Arjuna asks Krishna: what is a person of steady wisdom like? How do they speak, sit, walk?

Krishna's answer winds through craving and anger, and then, in paraphrase: one who moves among the things of the world with the senses in hand, free of grabbing and pushing away, comes to prasada, clearness.
In that clearness every sorrow ends, and for the one whose mind is clear, understanding soon stands steady. So here's the teaching, in Hindu terms: being well isn't only a body without a fever.
It reaches the self. A clear, settled mind is part of health, and part of the path, and Hindus seek it in daily prayer, in japa, in the quiet after a puja.
This path holds Sushruta's verse as a lens, not a checklist, and a real checkup still belongs with a doctor.
And that's the week: blessed hands, chanting for the sick, plants called mothers, the waters, Dhanvantari, food for a clear mind, and the word for well.

how: Ayurvedic teaching describes health as balance in the body together with a clear and content self, senses and mind, and Hindus seek that clearness (the Gita's prasada) in daily prayer and japa; on this path the description is a lens for noticing, not a medical assessment.

games.q: what does “the three doshas as a way of noticing” mean?
o: medicines that bring a sick body back to health
forces whose balance opens one old definition of health
a test that scores how healthy each person is

games.q: the word for well — tap the pairs.

s: in Sushruta's definition, health includes a clear and content mind
the one whose self, senses and mind are clear and content is called svastha.
the classical definition of health is only about the body
it starts with the doshas and digestion, then ends with self, senses and mind.
in the Gita, every sorrow ends in clearness of mind
in prasada, clearness, every sorrow ends, and understanding soon stands steady.

games.q: the fever's gone, but after a hard week your mind is still racing. by Sushruta and the Gita, are you svastha yet?
o: not all the way: svastha ends with a self, senses and mind that are clear
no: you're only healthy if you never get sick again
games.why: Sushruta's healthy person ends with prasanna: clear and content. and the Gita says in that clearness every sorrow ends.

practice: Start with the senses: what can you hear right now, and what can you see, even with your eyes half closed? Then the mind, busy or settled, with no grading, just a look.
Last, the simplest question: is there any clearness here at all, even a little? If you pray, rest there with a name of God. If you don't, simply rest with whatever is there.

wordCard.voice: The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Today, balanced doshas open Sushruta's definition of svastha, healthy, and a clear, content mind closes it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: healthy, well. Sushruta's word for the healthy person.

carryVoice: Your line: svastha: health that ends in a clear mind. In clearness, every sorrow ends. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 15 (the definition of the healthy person: balanced doshas, balanced fire, tissues and wastes working, self, senses and mind clear and content)
Bhagavad Gita 2.54 (Arjuna asks how the person of steady wisdom speaks, sits and walks)

Bhagavad Gita 2.64–65 (moving among objects with senses controlled, free of attraction and aversion, one reaches prasada; in it all sorrows end, and the understanding of the clear-minded soon becomes steady)
